Bumps sqlalchemy from 2.0.54 to 2.1.6.

Release notes
Sourced from sqlalchemy's releases.

2.1.6
Released: October 21, 2026
orm

[orm] [bug] Fixed issue where a Session flush that replaced an expired
object in the identity map with a newly flushed object of the same
primary key would emit a SELECT to refresh the expired object, solely in
order to determine whether to emit an "Identity map already had an
identity" warning.  This could occur when a row loaded within a
transaction is rolled back and its primary key value is subsequently
reused, and could lead to an AttributeError if the expired object
were garbage collected during that load.  The check now emits no SQL, and
an expired object that is replaced in this way no longer causes the
warning to be emitted.
This change is also backported to: 2.0.56
References: #13711

[orm] [bug] [regression] Fixed regression caused by #13070 where using more than one
orm.with_loader_criteria() option for the same entity, where the
criteria made use of correlated subqueries referring to that entity, would
fail with a RecursionError when compiling.
References: #13701

[orm] [bug] [regression] Fixed regression caused by the new implementation of .params() for
statements introduced in #7066, where parameter values passed to
the .params() method of an ORM statement created using
Select.from_statement() would not be applied when the statement
was compiled without the compiled statement cache, such as when the cache
was disabled or when the statement was stringified directly, leading to
an error that a value is required for the bound parameter.
References: #13709

orm extensions

[bug] [orm extensions] Fixed an issue in the instrumentation_toplevel extension where
unrelated classes inheriting from typing.Generic could incorrectly
raise a TypeError when using different instrumentation implementations.
Pull request courtesy TomasCaruso10.
This change is also backported to: 2.0.56

Release notes
Sourced from mkdocs-material's releases.

mkdocs-material-9.8.0

[!WARNING]
Material for MkDocs reaches end of life on May 5, 2027. Critical fixes and security updates continue until that date.
We're continuing our work with Zensical, a maintained successor built by the team behind Material for MkDocs. It carries forward what we've learned from building documentation tools with this community, with Markdown authoring, a familiar design, and full control over your content. Zensical is Open Source and MIT-licensed.
You can evaluate Zensical alongside MkDocs using your existing mkdocs.yml. Check plugin compatibility and compare your pages, navigation, search, and customizations before switching. The classic theme variant preserves the appearance of Material for MkDocs. See the migration guide for the steps and current compatibility details.
Upcoming changes on November 5

This is primarily a security release. It raises dependency minimums to address known vulnerabilities. We recommend upgrading to this release and updating your dependency lockfiles.
Python 3.11 or newer is now required. Python 3.8–3.10 are no longer supported.

Updated Node build-time dependencies to fix vulnerabilities
Updated Python dependency minimums and required Python 3.11
Removed RSS from recommended dependencies
Updated project status and maintenance links
Updated CLI notice with end-of-life and migration guidance
Removed redirects from recommended dependencies

Previous dependency ranges allowed versions with known vulnerabilities. The new minimums cover core Python dependencies and the optional git and imaging extras, including GitPython 3.2.1 or newer for the git extra.
Recent releases of mkdocs-rss-plugin and mkdocs-redirects depend on ProperDocs, a separate static site generator that Material for MkDocs does not require. Removing these plugins from the recommended extra keeps its dependency footprint smaller and leaves the choice of additional tools to each project. If your project uses RSS feeds or redirects, declare the relevant plugin explicitly in your own dependencies.
The CLI notice now gives the May 5, 2027 end-of-life date and links to the Zensical migration guide. It also clarifies that third-party ProperDocs migration notices do not represent a recommendation from the Material for MkDocs team. Package metadata now marks the project as inactive and includes maintenance and migration links.

#629: Fixed mocker.resetall() skipping the mocks patched with mocker.patch.multiple(), both the ones it creates and the ones passed explicitly.
#630: mocker.resetall() now also resets spy_return and spy_exception of spies, like it already did for spy_return_list and spy_return_iter, and no longer overwrites attributes with these names on mocks that are not spies.
#633: Fixed spies on classmethod, staticmethod, builtins and classes returning a MagicMock instead of calling the spied code after mocker.resetall(side_effect=True). Resetting a spy's side_effect now goes back to calling the spied code, also clearing any side_effect set on the spy.

Added a visualization tool to the Bodo query profile aggregator to generate graphs based on profiles.

body:
Bumps huggingface-hub from 2.0.0 to 2.3.0.

Release notes
Sourced from huggingface-hub's releases.

[v2.3.0] Bucket live-follow, faster HfFileSystem listings and more
🔄 Keep Bucket listings fresh with live_follow=True
HfFileSystem caches directory listings, so files added to a Bucket by another process did not show up until you called invalidate_cache(). With live_follow=True, HfFileSystem opens one background connection per listed Bucket to receive its file changes from the Hub. When a change arrives, it removes the cached listings it affects.
>>> from huggingface_hub import HfFileSystem
>>> hffs = HfFileSystem(live_follow=True)
>>> hffs.ls("buckets/my-username/my-bucket/data", detail=False)  # starts following that bucket
>>> # ... another process uploads a file to the bucket ...
>>> hffs.ls("buckets/my-username/my-bucket/data", detail=False)  # refreshed as changes arrive
['buckets/my-username/my-bucket/data/train.csv', 'buckets/my-username/my-bucket/data/new-file.csv']
It also works through fsspec with fsspec.filesystem("hf", live_follow=True), and through the storage_options argument of libraries such as pandas and pyarrow. The option is off by default because it keeps a connection open for each followed Bucket. It only affects listings and metadata (ls, info, exists, glob, ...), because reading a file always fetches its content from the Hub. It is not available for model, dataset and Space repos: use refresh=True to see a new commit.

[HfFileSystem] Add live-follow for Buckets by @​lhoestq in #5096

🚀 HfFileSystem lists large repos in parallel
Recursive listings such as find and glob used to be slow on large repos. The Hub returns a repo's file tree 1000 entries at a time, and each page can only be requested after the previous one has arrived. Listing datasets/allenai/objaverse (~800k files) took ~800 requests in a row, about 13 minutes.
HfFileSystem now splits recursive listings by sub-directory and lists them in parallel, with almost the same number of requests. A sub-tree that fits in a single page is never split. maxdepth is now applied during the listing, so the Hub only returns the levels you ask for.

datasets/allenai/objaverse
before
after

find(), 798,924 files
801 requests, 776 s
807 requests, 19.7 s

find(maxdepth=2), 328 entries
801 requests, 776 s
6 requests, 1.5 s

>>> from huggingface_hub import hffs
>>> files = hffs.glob("datasets/allenai/objaverse/**/*.glb", maxdepth=3)
The new max_workers argument of HfFileSystem sets the number of concurrent requests. It defaults to 16. Set it to 1 to list sequentially like before.

[HfFileSystem] List large repos in parallel by @​lhoestq in #5153

📎 Attach images and videos to discussions and PRs
The new HfApi.upload_attachment(path) uploads an image, video or audio file and returns its URL, which you can embed in a discussion, PR description or comment. Before, this required calling an undocumented Hub endpoint by hand.
>>> from huggingface_hub import HfApi
>>> api = HfApi()
>>> url = api.upload_attachment("screenshot.png")
>>> api.comment_discussion("username/repo-name", 5, f"Here is the fix:\n\n![screenshot](https://github.com/huggingface/huggingface_hub/blob/HEAD/{url})")

body:
Closes #4191
Rationale for this change
add_files infers a file's partition from the parquet min and max of the source column. That ignores the null count. A file holding 'a' and NULL has min = max = 'a', so it is registered under partition 'a'. s IS NULL then prunes it, and the scan in the issue returns [] instead of [2].
A value and NULL are two partition values, just as 'a' and 'b' are. add_files already refuses a file holding 'a' and 'b'. This change refuses a file holding a value and NULL in the same way, using the null count that is already in DataFileStatistics. A file whose column is all NULL still goes to the NULL partition, as before.
This PR covers only the value-and-NULL case. The issue mentions two other cases, and I left both alone:

NaN next to a value. Parquet statistics leave NaN out of min/max, and nan_value_counts is not filled from parquet metadata, so this check cannot see NaN.
No column statistics (write.metadata.metrics.default=none). The file gets a None partition, and mkdocs/docs/api.md documents that behavior. Changing it is a call for maintainers.

Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_add_files_refuses_partition_value_with_nulls in tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py runs on each catalog fixture:

It adds an all-'a' file and an all-NULL file, and checks that s = 'a' and s IS NULL return the right rows.
It then checks that a file holding 'a' and NULL is refused and nothing is added.

The test fails on main (no error is raised) and passes with this change. Unit tests (tests/ without integration and cloud suites): 4495 passed; the 4 failures are Kerberos tests in tests/catalog/test_hive.py that fail the same way on main in my environment. ruff check and ruff format --check are clean.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes. add_files now raises ValueError for a file where an identity-partition source column, or one with an order-preserving transform, holds both values and NULLs. Before, such a file was silently given the wrong partition.
title: Refuse add_files partition inference for a file holding a value and NULL

body:
Closes #4200
Rationale for this change
Currently, ExpireSnapshots._commit determines protected snapshots from the table's loaded metadata and sends no table requirements (self._requirements = ()). When another transaction concurrently moves or rolls back a branch/tag (such as rolling back main to the snapshot being expired), the expiration commit succeeds and RemoveSnapshotsUpdate silently deletes that ref. In the case of main, the table completely loses its main branch and reads as empty.
This change adds AssertRefSnapshotId requirements to self._requirements for each ref protecting snapshots. If a protected ref has changed concurrently, catalog validation fails with CommitFailedException instead of removing the ref or leaving the table in an inconsistent state.
Are these changes tested?
Yes, tested via unit and integration tests in tests/table/test_expire_snapshots.py:

test_expire_snapshots_asserts_ref_snapshot_id_requirements: verifies that AssertRefSnapshotId is staged for all protected refs.
test_expire_snapshots_concurrent_rollback_fails: end-to-end integration test with SqlCatalog verifying that concurrent rollback onto an expired snapshot fails with CommitFailedException and preserves main and its rows.

Are there any user-facing changes?
No breaking API changes. Concurrent snapshot expiration safely raises CommitFailedException if a protected branch or tag changed during the operation.
title: Fix: assert ref snapshot id requirements during snapshot expiration (#4200)

body:
Closes #4198
Rationale for this change
UpdateSpec checks each new partition name against the schema it was loaded with, using the check from #2305. Its commit asserts only the last assigned partition id and the default spec id. Suppose another writer adds a column xb in between. A stale handle can then add a partition field named xb, and the commit goes through. Java then refuses to load that metadata (Cannot create identity partition sourced from different field in schema: xb).
This change runs validate_partition_name again when AddPartitionSpecUpdate is applied, against the schema of the metadata the spec is being added to. On a catalog that applies updates to the latest metadata at commit time, the stale update_spec now raises the same ValueError it raises without the concurrent change. The schema-side check in UpdateSchema already validates every partition spec in this way.
The issue also mentions the opposite order: a stale update_schema().add_column("xb") after another writer added partition field xb. That is the same problem, but on the schema update path. I kept it out of this PR so this one stays small, and can follow up if wanted.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_concurrent_update_spec_checks_names_against_current_schema in tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py follows the issue's steps:

One handle adds column xb.
A stale handle then adds a bucket partition field named xb.
The test expects the ValueError, and checks that the table is still unpartitioned.

It fails on main (no error is raised) and passes with this change, for all catalog fixtures. Unit tests (tests/ without integration and cloud suites): 4501 passed; the 4 failures are Kerberos tests in tests/catalog/test_hive.py that fail the same way on main in my environment. ruff check and ruff format --check are clean.
Are there any user-facing changes?
A stale update_spec() that adds a partition field whose name now clashes with a column in the current schema raises ValueError at commit. Before, it wrote metadata that Java refuses to load.
title: Check partition names against the current schema when adding a spec

body:
Closes #4267
Rationale for this change
The spec's column projection rules fill a field that is missing from a data file from the identity partition value in the manifest. ArrowProjectionVisitor.struct applied that rule only inside the branch for optional fields and fields with an initial-default, so a required identity partition column raised ResolveError instead. Tables whose writers keep partition columns out of the data files, such as Hive-style layouts and tables converted from Delta, hit this on every read.
A required field now takes the projected value. A null partition value raises ResolveError for a required field, even when the field has an initial-default, unless the field's parent struct is null in every row.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_identity_transform_column_projection_required_field covers the projected value, the column's non-nullable type and row filters on it, with and without an initial-default, plus the null partition value. test_identity_transform_column_projection_required_field_under_null_parent covers a required child of an optional struct. Both fail without the change.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Scans of such tables return the partition value instead of raising ResolveError.
title: Project identity partition values into required columns missing from the data file

body:
Closes #2422
Rationale for this change
S3V4RestSigner adds the headers returned by the signing service with add_header, which appends. A header the request already had, such as X-Amz-Content-SHA256 set by botocore, is then sent twice: once with the original value and once with the signed value. The signature only covers the signed value, so stricter S3-compatible stores reject the request. The same duplication was measured in #3896.
This deletes the existing header (case-insensitive) before adding the signed value, so each signed header is sent once, with the value the signer returned.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_s3v4_rest_signer_replaces_existing_headers in tests/io/test_fsspec.py sends a request that already has X-Amz-Content-SHA256 and User-Agent, and checks that after signing each header appears once with the signed value. It fails on main and passes with this change. All signer tests in the file pass.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Signed S3 requests no longer carry duplicate headers. No configuration changes.
title: Replace S3 remote signer headers instead of appending them

body:
Rationale for this change
Appending to a table with an identity partition on a double or float column writes some rows twice when the data holds both -0.0 and 0.0. Signed zeros are easy to get, for example by rounding small negative values:
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.compute as pc

df = pa.table({"id": [1, 2, 3], "reading": pc.round(pa.array([-0.04, 0.04, 1.23]), 1)})
# reading: [-0.0, 0.0, 1.2]

tbl = catalog.create_table("default.readings", schema=df.schema)
with tbl.update_spec() as update:
    update.add_identity("reading")
tbl.append(df)
On main (and on 0.12.0), the three rows come back as five:
rows appended: 3
rows scanned:  5
ids scanned:   [1, 1, 2, 2, 3]
file {'reading': -0.0} record_count 2
file {'reading': 0.0} record_count 2
file {'reading': 1.2} record_count 1

With this change:
rows appended: 3
rows scanned:  3
ids scanned:   [1, 2, 3]
file {'reading': -0.0} record_count 1
file {'reading': 0.0} record_count 1
file {'reading': 1.2} record_count 1

_determine_partitions groups the rows by partition value, then selects each group's rows with pc.field(name) == value. group_by keeps -0.0 and 0.0 as two groups, but -0.0 == 0.0 is true, so each of the two filters selects the rows of both groups, and those rows are written into both data files. #4030 fixed the NaN case of this filter, where NaN never equals itself and its partition came out empty. This PR handles the opposite case: for a zero partition value, the filter also matches the sign of zero, using 1 / x, which is -inf for -0.0 and inf for 0.0.
The partitioning itself is unchanged. -0.0 and 0.0 are still two partitions, as before. Each row now lands in exactly one of them.
overwrite() and dynamic_partition_overwrite() write through the same function and had the same problem (3 rows in, 5 read back). Both return 3 rows with this change.
Are these changes tested?
Yes.

tests/io/test_pyarrow.py::test_determine_partitions_identity_signed_zero checks, for both double and float, that the -0.0, 0.0 and 1.0 rows each land in exactly one partition. On main, both zero partitions hold rows [1, 2, 4].
tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py::test_append_signed_zero_to_identity_partitioned_table appends to a real table (memory and SQL catalogs). It checks that a full scan returns each row once and that value = 0 returns both zero rows. On main, the scan returns [1, 1, 2, 2, 3].

All 4 new test cases fail on main and pass with the fix.
What I ran locally:

the whole of tests/io/test_pyarrow.py and tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py: 931 passed, 3 skipped;
the partition, append and overwrite tests in tests/table/test_partitioning.py and tests/catalog/test_sql.py: 31 passed;
ruff, ruff-format, mypy and codespell on the changed files.

I also checked the new filter expression on pyarrow 18.0.0, the minimum supported version. CI covers the rest of the suite and the integration tests.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes, a bug fix. Appending, overwriting or dynamically overwriting data that holds both -0.0 and 0.0 into an identity-partitioned float or double column no longer writes those rows twice. Rows that were already duplicated in existing tables stay as they are.
title: Write each row once when an identity partition has both -0.0 and 0.0

Closes #3680
Rationale for this change
TruncateTransform.satisfies_order_of reads self.source_type, but _source_type is never set on TruncateTransform, so comparing two truncate transforms with different widths raises:
AttributeError: 'TruncateTransform' object has no attribute '_source_type'

Following review feedback, this now matches the Java Truncate.satisfiesOrderOf: a truncate transform satisfies the order of another truncate transform when its width is greater than or equal to the other's. It no longer reads the missing source_type.
I left the source_type property in place to avoid an API change.
This picks up the same bug as #3681, #3682 and #3854, which the stale bot closed.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_truncate_satisfies_order_of_different_widths in tests/test_transforms.py covers equal widths, both directions of different widths, and other transform types. tests/test_transforms.py passes locally, and ruff check and ruff format pass.
Are there any user-facing changes?
TruncateTransform(a).satisfies_order_of(TruncateTransform(b)) now returns a >= b instead of raising AttributeError when a != b.

This change was prepared with an AI coding assistant, and the tests were run locally. The commits have a Generated-by: trailer, following the ASF generative tooling guidance. I've also reviewed the changes myself.

Rationale for this change
The spec resolves fields by ID and asks readers to be permissive: its manifest read rules say a field the reader's version doesn't define should be ignored ("Ignore the field"). Iceberg Java/Spark, DuckDB, and Snowflake skip unknown manifest fields of any type. PyIceberg skipped them only when they were primitives. A file-only map, list, or struct instead raised ResolveError: File/read schema are not aligned for map, got None, because SchemaPartnerAccessor raised whenever the partner was None. As a result, PyIceberg couldn't scan tables whose manifests carry extra nested fields, which other readers handle.
With this change, the accessor returns None for the children of a field that has no partner, and the existing None handling in ReadSchemaResolver reads and drops them. A real type mismatch, such as a map in the file and a string in the read schema, still raises.

body:
Part of #4291.
Rationale for this change
A partial Table.delete rewrites each data file that might hold matching rows. It reads the whole file with AlwaysTrue() and writes back the rows that don't match. The files to rewrite were planned with the delete filter, though, and that plan also leaves out delete files whose column bounds can't match the filter. For a filtered read that's correct, because the residual drops those rows anyway. For a full-file rewrite it isn't: the left-out delete files are never applied, so the rows they deleted come back in the new data file.
overwrite(..., overwrite_filter=...), dynamic_partition_overwrite and upsert go through Transaction.delete, so they're affected too.
The fix keeps the delete filter for choosing data files, but stops pruning delete files by their column bounds when planning a rewrite:

ManifestGroupPlanner takes a private _ignore_residuals: bool = False, like Java's ignoreResiduals. When it's True, the metrics evaluator is applied to data entries only, and every task's residual is AlwaysTrue. Partition pruning is unchanged, since a delete file only applies to data files in its own partition.
Transaction.delete plans its rewrite from the branch head with _ignore_residuals=True. It always planned locally, so server-side planning isn't involved. Transaction._scan is no longer used, so it's removed.

Scans keep the default, so reads and their planning cost are unchanged.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_partial_delete_keeps_earlier_deletes_outside_the_filter in tests/table/test_init.py runs against each catalog fixture and follows case 1 from the issue:

it commits a position delete that stores the deleted row (2, 'b'), which gives it bounds k = 2;
it checks that a scan for k = 1 leaves that delete file out;
it runs delete("k = 1") and checks only k = 3 is left.

Without the fix the final assertion fails with [2, 3] == [3]: the deleted row is back. PyIceberg can't write delete manifests yet, so the test reuses commit_partition_position_delete from tests/table/test_commit_retry.py, which now takes an optional row. Once #4002 lands, the helper can write the delete manifest without patching the snapshot producer.
The equality-delete case from the issue isn't tested here, because PyIceberg can't read equality deletes. With this change, a partial delete over a file that has an equality delete now reaches the existing "does not yet support equality deletes" error instead of silently writing the deleted rows back.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Partial deletes, filtered overwrites and upserts no longer resurrect rows removed by earlier delete files. A partial delete on a table with equality delete files that only the column bounds used to exclude now raises the existing unsupported-equality-deletes error, rather than writing incorrect data.
Not in this PR: the issue also points out that the retry conflict check (_filter_manifest_entries in table/update/validate.py) prunes delete entries the same way. That's a separate code path, so it will be fixed in a follow-up.
title: Apply every delete file when rewriting files for a partial delete

body:
Closes #4294
Rationale for this change
The problem
update_table_metadata ends in new_metadata.model_copy(deep=True). Every call therefore copies the entire table history: each snapshot with its summary, each snapshot log and metadata log entry, and each schema, partition spec and sort order. The cost of one call grows linearly with the number of snapshots the table keeps, regardless of how small the update is.
The function sits on the hot path of every write:

Transaction.table_metadata calls it on every read. One append reads the property 22 times.
Catalog._update_and_stage_table calls it once more on every commit. It is used by the SQL, Hive and Glue catalogs.

Each commit also adds a snapshot, so a table that receives frequent small commits pays a little more on each one. #4294 calls this quadratic in total.
How we ran into it
On a production table with a few thousand snapshots retained, a single fast_append commit took close to 10 seconds. Profiling the commit with cProfile and py-spy attributed 71% of its time to update_table_metadata → model_copy(deep=True) → copy.deepcopy, with about 4 million deepcopy calls per commit.
The cost tracks retention: in a reproduction with a larger history, the same commit took 18 s with 10,000 snapshots and 68 s with 40,000. A writer that commits frequently cannot keep up at that depth.
Why the deep copy exists, and why a shallow container copy is enough
The deep copy was introduced in #182 so that the metadata returned by update_table_metadata cannot change the base metadata. test_metadata_isolation_from_illegal_updates pins that guarantee. It appends to new_metadata.partition_specs and asserts that base_metadata.partition_specs is unchanged. As the test's own comment notes, Pydantic's frozen config cannot prevent mutations such as a list append.
That guarantee only requires the list and dict fields of TableMetadata to be distinct objects. The models they hold (Snapshot, Schema, PartitionSpec, SortOrder, SnapshotRef, the log entries) are themselves frozen, so they can be shared safely.
This is also how the Java implementation works. TableMetadata.Builder copies each collection (Lists.newArrayList(base.snapshots()), Maps.newHashMap(base.refs), and so on) and shares the immutable elements.
The handlers behind _apply_table_update were already required not to mutate their input in place: the first handler receives the base metadata itself, and the isolation test checks that the base is unchanged after legal updates. We audited all 23 handlers on main and found that each one builds new collections or returns its input unchanged. This change adds no new requirement on them.
The change
The final model_copy(deep=True) is replaced by a copy of the list and dict fields alone, sharing everything else:
return new_metadata.model_copy(
    update={name: value.copy() for name, value in new_metadata if isinstance(value, (list, dict))}
)
There is no cache and no change to the API, and the enforce_validation path is untouched. Fixing the function rather than its callers makes every path cheap: reads with or without staged updates, and the commit inside each catalog.

Working towards #3222

Rationale for this change
We need to be able to read data files encrypted with Parquet Modular Encryption.

A data file's key_metadata in its manifest entry holds the plaintext key and AAD prefix for that file. The manifest holding it is itself encrypted, so this doesn't need the EncryptionManager or the KMS.
When key_metadata is set, scans build the Parquet file format with decryption properties from PyArrow's direct key API, pyarrow.parquet.encryption.create_decryption_properties (apache/arrow#49667). This matches iceberg-rust, which builds arrow-rs FileDecryptionProperties from the key and AAD prefix ([9/N] apache/iceberg-rust#2584).
This covers data files and Parquet position delete files. Encrypted ORC files raise, and deletion vectors come in a follow-up.
The AAD prefix always comes from key metadata, because Java doesn't store it in the file.

The direct key API was added in PyArrow 25, so reading an encrypted file on an older PyArrow raises an ImportError asking for 25.0.0 or later. The minimum PyArrow version for everything else is unchanged.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. A Parquet data file encrypted by iceberg-rust is checked in under tests/table/encryption, and reading it with its key metadata returns its rows. There's also a round trip of an encrypted data file with an encrypted position delete file. Reads fail with a wrong key, a wrong AAD prefix, missing key metadata, or key metadata on a plaintext file.
Are there any user-facing changes?
No. Nothing changes for unencrypted tables.
title: feat(encryption): [11/N] Read encrypted Parquet data files

body:
Closes #4290
Rationale for this change

A REST server can advertise idempotency-key-lifetime, after which clients send an Idempotency-Key (UUIDv7) on mutations and reuse it on retry, so a retried commit can't apply twice. PyIceberg sent no key and never retried POST.
With the lifetime advertised, each mutation now carries a fresh key, and the rest.client.* retry policy also covers POST, reusing the key across retries, as Java's RESTSessionCatalog does.
The lifetime itself isn't enforced: urllib3 retries are bounded and finish well within typical lifetimes.

Are these changes tested?

test_rest.py — mutations carry a UUIDv7 key only when advertised, a different one per operation, and reads carry none; a POST retried after a 503 reuses its key.

Are there any user-facing changes?

Against servers that advertise idempotency-key-lifetime, mutations send Idempotency-Key and POST is retried under rest.client.*.
title: feat: send Idempotency-Key on REST mutations when the server advertises it

body:
Closes #4312
Rationale for this change
data_file_statistics_from_parquet_metadata built a column's bounds from the row groups that report a min/max and silently skipped a row group whose statistics have no min/max. PyArrow writes such statistics when a value is larger than 4 KB. The stored bounds then exclude that row group's values, and the metrics evaluator prunes the file from scans that should match it.
With this change, a row group that holds non-null values but reports no min/max drops the column's bounds for the file. The column keeps its null and value counts, because the row group still reports them. A row group whose values are all null still has no effect on the bounds.
Are these changes tested?

Are there any user-facing changes?
Data files written from now on have no bounds for such a column, so scans no longer skip their matching rows. Files already written keep their bounds.

tbl.append(pa.table({"qty": pa.array([1, 2], pa.int32())}))
with tbl.update_schema() as u:
    u.update_column("qty", field_type=LongType())

tbl.inspect.files()
# 0.11.1:  struct.error: unpack requires a buffer of 8 bytes

body:
Closes #4183
Rationale for this change
A transaction that writes two refs only guarded the first one against concurrent changes.
Transaction._stage de-duplicated requirements by type alone, so after the first write staged
AssertRefSnapshotId(ref="b"), the second write's AssertRefSnapshotId(ref="main") was dropped and
the commit reached the catalog without an assertion on main.
The type-only de-duplication was correct when it was added (#569), because a transaction could only
ever assert main. Writing to branches (#941) made AssertRefSnapshotId per-ref, but the
de-duplication was never updated.
This changes the key to (type, ref) for AssertRefSnapshotId. Each ref keeps its first (base)
assertion, matching Java's UpdateRequirements. Other requirement types are unchanged. Retries go
through _stage too, so they now keep every ref's assertion as well.
cat.load_table("ns.t").manage_snapshots().rollback_to_snapshot(s1).commit()   # another writer
with t.transaction() as tx:
    tx.append(row(3), branch="b")
    tx.append(row(3))

cat.load_table("ns.t").scan()   # before: [1, 2, 3]  rollback silently undone
                                # after:  [1, 3]     conflict detected, commit retried
Measured on a transaction that writes branch b and then main:

Concurrent change to main
Format
Before
After

rollback
v1 / v2
rollback undone
retried, [1, 3]

append
v1
appended row lost
retried, [1, 2, 3, 4]

append
v2
non-retryable ValueError (sequence number)
retried, [1, 2, 3, 4]

Are these changes tested?
Yes. Two tests were added to tests/table/test_commit_retry.py, and each runs against every catalog
fixture:

test_transaction_writing_two_branches_detects_concurrent_change_to_either covers the issue's
scenario on format v1 and v2, with both a concurrent rollback and a concurrent append.
test_transaction_stages_one_ref_assertion_per_ref checks that writing b and then main twice
stages exactly one assertion per ref, each holding the base snapshot id.

Both fail when the _stage change is reverted. Unit suite: 4524 → 4530 passed, no new failures.
make lint is clean. make test-integration passes (1362 passed, 0 failed).
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes, as a bug fix. Multi-ref transactions now detect concurrent changes to every ref they write, and
retry or fail with CommitFailedException instead of overwriting them. There is no API change.
title: Assert every ref a transaction writes, not just the first

body:
Closes #4316

Draft: depends on #4315. This branch is stacked on #4315, so the first commit
(Assert every ref a transaction writes, not just the first) belongs to that PR. Only the last commit
is new here. Without #4315, a conflict on a second branch never triggers a retry, so the path fixed
here can't be reached. I'll rebase onto main once #4315 merges.

Rationale for this change
When a transaction writes more than one branch, concurrency validation for a write on a later branch
was computed from the first write's branch. Both places that build a CommitWindow resolved a
single window from self._snapshot_producers[0] and reused it for every producer:

Transaction._rebuild_snapshot_updates (the retry path, reported in #4316);
the empty-staged-output path in Transaction.commit_transaction (a delete whose plan matched
nothing). Same root cause, found while fixing the first.

If the first branch didn't change concurrently, its window is empty, so a serializable delete or
overwrite on the second branch skipped validation and committed over a conflicting change it never saw.
tx = t.transaction()
tx.append(pa.table({"x": [9]}))              # main
tx.delete("x == 1", branch="b")              # serializable delete on b
cat.load_table("ns.t").append(pa.table({"x": [1]}), branch="b")   # concurrent matching append to b
tx.commit_transaction()
# before: commits, conflict missed (the delete alone raises)
# after:  ValidationException, same as the single-branch delete
This adds Transaction._resolve_commit_windows(), which resolves one window per target branch,
based on the first producer that writes to that branch, and uses it in both places.
Why not simply a window per producer? A producer's _starting_snapshot_id is its branch head as the
transaction sees it. For a second write to the same branch, that's the snapshot staged by the first
write, which the catalog has never seen, so resolving it fails with Cannot find starting snapshot.
(Transaction.delete already pins its overwrite's start to the delete's for the same reason.) The
first producer on each branch always starts from a committed snapshot.
Single-branch transactions behave exactly as before: there, the first producer on the branch is
producer 0.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. Three tests were added to tests/table/test_commit_retry.py, and each runs against every catalog
fixture:

test_retry_validates_each_branch_against_its_own_commits: the #4316 scenario (retry path) raises
ValidationException and leaves both branches untouched.
test_empty_plan_validation_checks_each_branch_against_its_own_commits: the same bug in the
empty-output path.
test_retry_with_two_writes_to_one_branch_succeeds: a guard that a second write to the same branch
still retries successfully. It fails with Cannot find starting snapshot under a naive
per-producer window.

The first two fail before the change and the third passes. Unit suite against the #4315 base:
4530 → 4539 passed, no new failures. make lint is clean.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes, as a bug fix. Multi-branch transactions now validate each branch's writes against that branch's
concurrent commits, so a conflicting serializable delete or overwrite raises ValidationException
instead of committing. There is no API change.
title: Validate each branch against its own commits on retry

body:
Closes #4187
Rationale for this change
ManageSnapshots.create_branch and create_tag set the ref without checking whether the name exists, so an existing branch was reset to the given snapshot and lost its commits, and an existing tag moved. remove_branch and remove_tag checked nothing either: a missing name was accepted, a tag could be removed as a branch, and remove_branch("main") left the table reading as empty.
The names are now checked against the refs as they stand after earlier operations in the same chain (_effective_refs), and the error messages match Java's UpdateSnapshotReferencesOperation: Ref x already exists, Cannot remove main branch, Branch does not exist: x, Tag does not exist: x, Ref x is a tag not a branch, Ref x is a branch not a tag. Replacing a ref on purpose is still possible with remove_branch(...).create_branch(...) in one chain.
AI assistance was used for the analysis and drafting; the change was reviewed and tested by the author.

Four unit tests in tests/table/test_manage_snapshots.py: an existing name is refused for both kinds, a name staged earlier in the same chain is refused, every remove_* refusal, and remove-then-create of the same name in one chain still commits both updates in order. The script from the issue now raises Ref dev already exists and Ref v1 already exists, and dev keeps [1, 2]. make lint and make test pass.

body:
Closes #4323
Rationale for this change
PartitionFieldStats.update takes bounds with Python's min and max, which keep whichever of -0.0 and 0.0 came first. The spec says the lower bound must not be +0.0 when -0.0 is a value, and the upper bound must not be -0.0 when +0.0 is a value: https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#manifest-lists
After min and max, a zero now replaces a zero bound of the other sign when it belongs there, so -0.0 sorts below 0.0. That is the order Iceberg Java's PartitionSummary gets from Double.compareTo. Nonzero floats and other types take the same path as before.
StatsAggregator in pyiceberg/io/pyarrow.py aggregates data file column bounds with the same min and max. For files PyIceberg writes this is already correct, because Arrow's Parquet writer stores a zero minimum as -0.0 and a zero maximum as +0.0, already in pyarrow 18.0.0, the oldest version PyIceberg supports: https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/apache-arrow-18.0.0/cpp/src/parquet/statistics.cc#L338-L367. Files from other writers added with add_files may not follow that rule, which I'll raise separately.
#4274 is a different signed zero bug, on the write path, and doesn't overlap with this.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_construct_partition_summaries_orders_negative_zero_below_zero builds the summary for [0.0, -0.0] and [-0.0, 0.0], for float and double fields, and fails on main. make lint passes. make test passes apart from four Kerberos tests in tests/catalog/test_hive.py, which need puresasl, and that isn't installed here.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes. Manifest lists for float and double partition fields that hold both zeros now get the bounds the spec requires. There is no API change. Please add the changelog label.

body:
What's changed
StatsAggregator.update_min/update_max aggregate parquet row-group statistics into DataFile.lower_bounds/upper_bounds. On a tie between +0.0 and -0.0, min(val, current) and max(val, current) keep the first argument — so whichever zero arrives last wins:

a late -0.0 lowers an existing +0.0 upper bound (e.g. row group 1 contains +0.0, a later row group's max is -0.0),
a late +0.0 raises an existing -0.0 lower bound.

The serialized bounds then order above a value that is present in the file, violating the two's-comparable bound ordering.
#4324 fixed the same class in the partition-field summary path (PartitionFieldStats.update in manifest.py); this applies the equivalent guard to the data-file metrics path. The argument order here is flipped (min(val, current) vs min(self._min, value)), so the guarded directions are mirrored, and the guard is split across the two update methods. Verified against #4324's pinned bar: for both arrival orders the bounds must serialize as lower = to_bytes(-0.0), upper = to_bytes(+0.0).
NaN needs no handling here: pyarrow row-group statistics exclude NaN (has_min_max is False for all-NaN chunks), so the aggregator never sees it on this path.
Test
test_stats_aggregator_orders_negative_zero_below_zero — parametrized over both arrival orders and FloatType/DoubleType, asserting the serialized bounds match the #4324 canonical pair. Verified failing-first: 4/4 fail on main (533a617) and pass with the guard; the existing StatsAggregator tests (18) still pass.
AI disclosure: code and tests drafted with AI assistance, verified locally by running the full failing-first cycle.

body:
Rationale for this change
update_schema() updates the default name mapping, and _UpdateMapping removed a mapped name from an existing field whenever a new or renamed field claimed that name. For files without field ids those names are the only way a column is found, so the removal changed what an existing column reads.
After renaming a to b, the mapping for field 1 holds both names. Adding a new column a then stripped a from field 1 and gave it to the new field. Files added with add_files were read through the name mapping, so b started reading null and the new a received the old values. Dropping and re-adding a column had the same effect.
Existing names now stay on the field they were mapped to, and newly added fields are appended to the mapping. A name that a file was written with keeps resolving to the field id it was written for, which matches the behavior of files that carry field ids. Dropped fields keep their entry in the mapping for the same reason: their names must not start resolving to a later column with the same name.
Are these changes tested?
Yes.

tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py::test_add_column_keeps_values_of_renamed_column_without_field_ids adds a Parquet file without field ids, renames the column, adds a column with the old name, and asserts the renamed column still reads its values while the new one reads null. It runs against the memory, sql, and sql_without_rowcount catalogs and fails on main.
tests/table/test_name_mapping.py::test_update_mapping_keeps_name_of_existing_field covers the mapping directly, and the existing test_update_mapping now expects the old field to keep its name.

Full unit suite: 4564 passed, 5 skipped. prek run -a passes.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes. Adding a column no longer changes the values read from files without field ids, and a reused column name no longer re-attributes their data to the new column.
Closes #4318
title: Core: Keep mapped names of existing fields when a column is added

body:
Rationale for this change
Some REST catalogs expose only the current snapshot and keep table history elsewhere, Nessie being the main example. CommitWindow.resolve raised ValidationException: Cannot find starting snapshot <id> whenever the starting snapshot was missing after a refresh, so since the retry added in #3320 no commit loser could ever retry on those catalogs, not even a plain append.
The window now records that the starting snapshot is missing instead of raising:

Operations that need no conflict validation, such as appends, retry as they do anywhere else. _refresh_for_retry already rebuilds on the refreshed head, which is also what Java's SnapshotProducer does.
Operations that do validate, such as overwrites and deletes, cannot run the check without the history. They now raise CommitFailedException with a message saying the starting snapshot is not exposed, which is the pre-0.12 behavior and tells a lost race apart from a data conflict. They never continue without validation.

Are these changes tested?
Yes. New tests in tests/table/test_commit_retry.py hide the starting snapshot from the refreshed metadata to emulate a catalog without history:

test_append_retry_without_starting_snapshot races two appends and asserts the loser retries and both land.
test_delete_retry_without_starting_snapshot_raises_commit_failed asserts a delete raises CommitFailedException instead of ValidationException.
test_validate_concurrency_marks_missing_starting_snapshot covers the window flags directly.

All three fail on main and pass with the change. Full unit suite: 4570 passed, 5 skipped. prek run -a passes.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes. On catalogs that only expose the current snapshot, retried appends now succeed instead of raising ValidationException. Retried overwrites and deletes raise CommitFailedException again, as they did before 0.12, with a message that names the missing starting snapshot.
Closes #4327
title: Core: Retry appends on catalogs that only expose the current snapshot

body:
Rationale for this change
get_rows_to_update compared every matched row one cell at a time, slicing both tables and calling as_py() for each column. Cost grew with rows times columns: on a table with 200 columns and 20k matched rows the comparison alone took around 20 seconds, before anything was written.
The matched rows are now gathered once and compared column by column with PyArrow kernels. Two nulls count as equal, a null against a value counts as a change, and every row is still returned only once. Columns whose types have no comparison kernel, structs and lists today, fall back to the previous value-by-value comparison, so nested types behave as before.
The reproduction from the issue now takes about 0.1 seconds instead of about 20.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. New tests in tests/table/test_upsert.py cover get_rows_to_update directly:

only the changed rows are returned
a row is returned once even when several columns changed
two nulls compare equal while a null against a value is a change
struct columns are still compared

Full unit suite: 4570 passed, 5 skipped. prek run -a passes.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes, only in speed: upsert no longer slows down sharply with the number of columns. The returned rows are unchanged, except that two NaN values in the same column now compare equal, which matches Iceberg's comparator semantics.
Closes #3860
title: Core: Compare upsert rows column by column instead of cell by cell

body:
Rationale for this change
Planning a table repeatedly read the same immutable files from object storage every time: the manifest list on every plan_files, and every manifest on every plan. _manifest_cache only keeps the parsed ManifestFile records, not the file contents.
This adds a byte cache to FileIO, keyed by location. Parsing is unchanged; the bytes are cached, so a ManifestFile record parsed from one manifest list cannot be served values from another, which a parsed-object cache keyed by path would allow.
It follows Iceberg Java's io.manifest.cache-* properties and is off by default:

io.manifest.cache-enabled (default false)
io.manifest.cache.max-total-bytes (default 100 MiB)
io.manifest.cache.max-content-length (default 8 MiB)
io.manifest.cache.expiration-interval-ms (default 60 s)

ContentCache is a bounded, least-recently-used map with lazy expiry, matching the get(location) -> bytes | None and put(location, data) shape from the issue. A FileIO that wants a different backing store, a disk cache for example, can override FileIO.content_cache, which is read-only and returns None when the properties do not enable caching.
Only manifest lists and manifests go through the cache. Data files and metadata.json are unchanged, so nothing that can be rewritten is cached.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. tests/io/test_content_cache.py covers:

caching is off unless io.manifest.cache-enabled is truthy, including the values false, 0 and the empty string
the limits are read from FileIO properties, including table properties
entries over max-content-length, or over max-total-bytes on their own, are not cached
least-recently-used eviction and expiry

body:
Rationale for this change
SqlCatalog.__init__ always built its own engine from the uri property, and since 0.12 it also probes the catalog schema in the constructor. An application that already owns a configured Engine could only build the catalog from a URI and replace catalog.engine afterwards, which is too late: the probe has already run on PyIceberg's engine, without the pool, connect_args, SSL context, event listeners or wait callbacks the application set.
SqlCatalog now accepts an optional engine:
catalog = SqlCatalog("default", engine=engine, warehouse="s3://bucket/prefix")
When an engine is passed it is used as-is, uri is not required, and _init_catalog() runs on it, so the schema probe and table creation happen on the application's engine. Without an engine the behavior is unchanged: the engine is built from uri with the existing echo and pool_pre_ping properties.
Are these changes tested?

test_creation_with_existing_engine passes an engine, asserts the catalog keeps that exact object, asserts the catalog tables were created on it, and creates and finds a table.
test_creation_with_existing_engine_without_uri does the same without a uri property.

The existing test_creation_with_no_uri still covers the error when neither an engine nor a URI is given.
Full unit suite: 4562 passed, 5 skipped. prek run -a passes.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes. SqlCatalog takes a new optional engine argument. When it is given, uri becomes optional and is only kept in the catalog properties.
Closes #4322

body:
Rationale for this change
An append plans its data files against the table's partition spec, and each DataFile carries the spec_id it was planned with. When the commit is retried, the producer rebuilt its snapshot against the refreshed metadata and wrote every added file into a manifest using the refreshed default spec:
with self.new_manifest_writer(spec=self._transaction.table_metadata.spec()):
If another writer changed the partition spec in between, the manifest labelled the planned partitions with fields from the new spec. A file written with p=7 under spec 1 was then listed under spec 2 as q=7, so a filter on q pruned it, and when the specs had different numbers of fields the write raised IndexError. _summary() used the same refreshed default spec, so the partition summaries were mislabelled too.
Added files are now grouped by their own spec_id, one manifest per spec, and the snapshot summary uses the spec each file was planned with. This also covers files from add_files that belong to an older spec than the current default. Deleted files already used their own spec id for both the manifest and the summary.
Are these changes tested?
Yes, in tests/table/test_commit_retry.py:

test_retried_append_records_the_spec_it_was_planned_with changes the spec concurrently, asserts the retried append is found by a filter on the new spec's column, and asserts the new manifest keeps spec 1.
test_retried_append_with_a_spec_that_has_more_fields covers the IndexError case, where the refreshed spec has more fields than the planned one.

Both fail on main and pass with the change. The synthetic DataFiles in test_snapshot_producer_bounded_metadata_access now pass spec_id=0, like real data files do.
Full unit suite: 4568 passed, 5 skipped. prek run -a passes.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes. A retried append after a concurrent partition spec change now records its file under the spec it was written with, so filters on the new spec no longer prune it and the append no longer raises IndexError when the field counts differ.
Closes #4188
title: Core: Write added files under the partition spec they were planned with

body:
Rationale for this change
Transaction.commit_transaction only checked whether a failed attempt had actually landed before starting the next attempt. When the failure ended the loop instead, it raised straight into the handler that calls _clean_all_uncommitted() on every producer:

commit.retry.num-retries=0, so there is no next attempt.
A response lost on the final attempt.
The total retry timeout elapsing.

A catalog can apply a commit and still report CommitFailedException, for example when the response is lost or a transport retry gets a conflict for a request that already applied. The snapshot is then live while its manifest list and manifests have been deleted, so the table can no longer be scanned.
The landed check now runs before the cleanup on the last attempt too. It was also pulled into _attempt_landed(), which refreshes the table and looks for the producer's snapshot id, so both paths use the same check. If the refresh fails, the outcome is unknown, so it raises CommitStateUnknownException and the files are kept, which is how other unknown outcomes are already handled.
Are these changes tested?
Yes, in tests/table/test_commit_retry.py, by stubbing Catalog.commit_table to fail before ("conflict") or after ("lost") the real commit:

test_lost_response_on_the_last_attempt_keeps_the_landed_snapshot uses commit.retry.num-retries=0, appends, and asserts the append returns, exactly one snapshot exists, its manifest list is still on disk, and the rows scan back.
test_lost_response_on_the_final_retry_keeps_the_landed_snapshot loses the response on the second and last attempt after a real conflict on the first, and asserts the same.
test_unreadable_commit_outcome_raises_commit_state_unknown makes the refresh fail and asserts CommitStateUnknownException.

All three fail on main and pass with the change.
Full unit suite: 4575 passed, 5 skipped. prek run -a passes.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes. A commit whose response is lost after the catalog applied it no longer deletes the files of the snapshot it landed, so the table stays readable, and the call returns successfully instead of raising. When the outcome cannot be determined because the table cannot be refreshed, CommitStateUnknownException is raised and no files are deleted.
Closes #4021
title: Core: Check whether a failed last commit attempt landed before cleanup

body:
Rationale for this change
Appending a dictionary-encoded Arrow table to a table partitioned by bucket, truncate, year, month, day or hour raised:
ValueError: FeatureUnsupported => Unsupported data type for bucket transform: Dictionary(Int32, Utf8)

The partition transforms run on Arrow arrays through _pyiceberg_transform_wrapper, which forwarded the array as-is. The Arrow kernels behind the transforms have no implementation for dictionary types, so any dictionary-encoded column used in a partition transform failed even though Iceberg has no dictionary type and reads such a column as its value type.
The wrapper now decodes dictionary arrays with dictionary_decode() before calling the transform, per chunk for chunked arrays. The result matches what the same values produce without dictionary encoding, so partitions, and therefore partition pruning, stay the same.
Are these changes tested?
Yes.

tests/test_transforms.py::test_pyarrow_transform_decodes_dictionary_arrays covers both pa.Array and pa.ChunkedArray and asserts the dictionary-encoded input gives the same buckets as the plain input, including a null.
tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py::test_write_dictionary_encoded_column_with_bucket_partition appends a dictionary-encoded table to a bucket-partitioned table, checks the rows read back and that both partitions were created. It runs against the memory, sql, and sql_without_rowcount catalogs.

Both fail on main and pass with the change.
Full unit suite: 4573 passed, 5 skipped. prek run -a passes.
Are there any user-facing changes?

title: Core: Decode dictionary arrays before applying Arrow partition transforms

body:
Rationale for this change
A table can hold files with plain string columns and files with dictionary-encoded string columns, for example after a writer started passing dictionary-encoded Arrow tables. ArrowScan.to_table concatenates one table per batch with promote_options="permissive", which promotes large types but cannot merge a plain string column with a dictionary-encoded one, so the scan failed with:
pyarrow.lib.ArrowTypeError: Unable to merge: Field col has incompatible types: string vs dictionary<values=string, indices=int32, ordered=0>

Batches are now normalized before concatenation. Dictionary-encoded columns that were not requested through ArrowScan(dictionary_columns=...) are decoded to their value type, so every batch shares one logical schema. Columns that were explicitly requested as dictionary-encoded keep their dictionary type, which the existing dictionary_columns behavior and its test rely on.

The existing tests/io/test_pyarrow.py::test_dictionary_columns_produces_dict_encoded_output still passes, which guards that requested dictionary columns are not decoded.

Rationale for this change

body:
Rationale for this change
_determine_partitions adds the transformed partition values to the Arrow table as temporary columns named _partition_<partition field name>. If the data already has a column with that name, the lookup by name is ambiguous and append() fails:
schema = Schema(
    NestedField(1, "id", LongType()),
    NestedField(2, "_partition_region", StringType()),
    NestedField(3, "region", StringType()),
)
spec = PartitionSpec(PartitionField(source_id=3, field_id=1000, transform=IdentityTransform(), name="region"))
table = catalog.create_table("default.t", schema=schema, partition_spec=spec)
table.append(pa.table({"id": [1], "_partition_region": ["a"], "region": ["us"]}))
# KeyError: 'Field "_partition_region" exists 2 times in schema'
This change picks helper column names that are not already in the table, by prefixing underscores until the name is free. The helper columns are still dropped before the data files are written.

body:
Rationale for this change
delete() and overwrite() accept case_sensitive=False, and the operation binds its filter that way. When a concurrent commit lands first, the retry validates the filter against the new snapshots, but the helpers in pyiceberg/table/update/validate.py bind it with the default case_sensitive=True. A filter that matches the column only case-insensitively then fails, even when the concurrent commit does not conflict:
tbl1 = catalog.load_table("default.t")  # column "Id"
tbl2 = catalog.load_table("default.t")
tbl1.append(pa.table({"Id": [0]}))
tbl2.delete("id > 5", case_sensitive=False)
# ValueError: Could not find field with name id, case_sensitive=True
The same delete written with the exact column case commits. This change passes the operation's case_sensitive setting through the conflict-detection helpers to the metrics evaluator they use, as Java's MergingSnapshotProducer does with its caseSensitive flag. The new parameter defaults to True, so other callers are unchanged.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. Two tests in tests/table/test_commit_retry.py, run against each catalog of the catalog fixture, both fail without the fix:

test_concurrent_append_case_insensitive_delete_retries_successfully: after a non-conflicting concurrent append, the case-insensitive delete retries and commits.
test_concurrent_append_case_insensitive_delete_raises_validation_exception: a conflicting concurrent append still raises ValidationException, not ValueError.
test_snapshot_isolation_case_insensitive_delete_after_concurrent_delete_retries_successfully and ..._raises_validation_exception: the same under snapshot isolation after a concurrent delete, which reaches _validate_deleted_data_files.

test_added_delete_files_case_insensitive_filter in tests/table/test_validate.py covers _added_delete_files and _validate_no_new_delete_files with a mixed-case filter and case_sensitive=False.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Bug fix only: case-insensitive deletes and overwrites now retry after a concurrent commit instead of raising ValueError. No API changes.
This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.
title: Bind conflict-detection filters with the operation's case sensitivity

body:
Rationale for this change
Scans drop NaN rows for predicates that NaN satisfies: IsNaN, NotEqualTo and NotIn. Parquet statistics exclude NaN, so a row group whose non-NaN values are all equal reports min == max. pyarrow prunes that row group for is_nan(x), which is false for the value 7.0, and the scan never returns the NaN row:
# tbl: table with id (long) and x (double)
tbl.append(pa.table({"id": pa.array([0, 1], pa.int64()), "x": pa.array([float("nan"), 7.0], pa.float64())}))
tbl.scan(row_filter=IsNaN("x")).to_arrow()  # 0 rows; expected the row (0, NaN)
The trigger is a float or double row group with no nulls whose non-NaN values are all equal. Nulls in the same row group avoid it.
This change keeps NaN-sensitive predicates away from Parquet pruning. _task_to_record_batches pushes down only the top-level AND conjuncts that cannot hide NaN rows. A conjunct is NaN-sensitive if it is IsNaN, NotEqualTo, or NotIn on a float or double column. When one is present, each batch is filtered with the full expression after the read, as already happens for scans with positional deletes. NOT is left to a follow-up that applies rewrite_not before the Arrow conversion, as the metrics evaluators do. Upstream issue: apache/arrow#51491.
Trade-off: NaN-sensitive conjuncts lose Parquet row-group pruning, and other conjuncts keep it. Java's row-group filter takes the same conservative view: for notEq and notIn it never drops a row group, and for isNaN it drops one only when the column is all null (ParquetMetricsRowGroupFilter).
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_task_to_record_batches_keeps_nan_rows_for_nan_sensitive_filters in tests/io/test_pyarrow.py covers IsNaN, NotEqualTo, NotIn, AND, OR and NotNaN, each on a float and a double column. test_scan_nan_row_with_equal_finite_statistics in tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py runs the public scan path on the memory, sql, and sql_without_rowcount catalogs. Both fail without the fix and pass with it.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Bug fix only: scans return the NaN rows they previously dropped. No API changes.
This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.
title: Fix scans dropping NaN rows for IsNaN, NotEqualTo and NotIn

body:
Rationale for this change
Transaction.add_files(..., branch=...) checks for already-referenced files only against the current snapshot (main), not against the target branch. Adding the same file to a branch twice is therefore not rejected, and reading the branch returns the file's rows twice:
tbl.append(main_rows)
tbl.manage_snapshots().create_branch(snapshot_id=tbl.metadata.current_snapshot_id, branch_name="b").commit()
tbl.add_files([path], branch="b")
tbl.add_files([path], branch="b")  # should raise "already referenced by table"; it commits a second copy
The second call succeeds, and the branch holds two live entries for path. The same second call on main is rejected. #3287 describes this as a pre-existing inconsistency and preserved it.
This change makes the check cover the target branch's snapshot as well as the current snapshot. The existing main check stays, and a file the branch already references is now rejected too. Snapshots and manifests shared by both are read once.
Related: #3287
Are these changes tested?
Yes. The tests are in tests/integration/test_add_files.py and run against the memory and SQL catalogs. test_add_files_to_branch_rejects_file_already_referenced_by_branch and test_add_files_to_branch_rejects_file_added_earlier_in_transaction fail without this change (the second add is not rejected) and pass with it. test_add_files_to_branch_accepts_distinct_file_with_same_rows adds a different path with the same rows and passes both ways. test_add_files_to_branch_rejects_file_referenced_only_by_main passes both ways and pins that files referenced by main are still rejected on a branch.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes: add_files with a non-main branch now also rejects files that the branch already references. Files referenced by main are still rejected, and the check_duplicate_files docs mention the target branch.
This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.

body:
Rationale for this change
A decimal filter literal with more digits than the column's precision makes the scan fail, even though the filter is valid. Here amt is decimal(5, 2), so its largest value is 999.99:
tbl.scan(row_filter="amt < 1000.00").to_arrow()
# ArrowInvalid: Decimal type with precision 6 does not fit into precision inferred from first array element: 5
!=, IN and NOT IN with such a literal fail the same way. PyIceberg builds the Arrow literal with the column's type, decimal128(5, 2), which cannot hold 1000.00. Java compares by value here: its DecimalLiteral.to keeps the literal as is.
This change gives the Arrow literal of a decimal column a precision wide enough for its digits (decimal128(6, 2) here) and keeps the column's scale, for comparisons and for IN / NOT IN. When the literal fits, the Arrow type is unchanged.
Related to #4203 / #4210, which handle a column widened by schema evolution (old files keep the narrower type). This PR covers a literal wider than the table's own column type, which #4210 does not change. The two do not conflict: #4210 changes how the file-level filter is bound, this PR changes the Arrow type of decimal literals.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. Both new tests in tests/io/test_pyarrow.py fail with the ArrowInvalid above without the fix:

test_decimal_literal_wider_than_column_to_pyarrow converts <, !=, IN and NOT IN on a decimal(5, 2) column and evaluates them on an Arrow table.
test_row_filter_decimal_literal_wider_than_column scans an in-memory catalog table with amt < 1000.00, amt > -1000.00, amt IN (1.25, 1000.00) and amt < 50.00 (a literal that fits). A NULL row in the table matches none of them.

Are there any user-facing changes?
Bug fix only: a decimal literal wider than the column's precision no longer makes the scan raise ArrowInvalid. No API changes.
This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.
title: Widen decimal literal precision in scan filters

body:
Rationale for this change
The manifest and metrics evaluators apply rewrite_not, so not value < 6.0 decides which files are read as value >= 6.0. The rows of those files were then filtered with the original expression, which Arrow evaluates as ~(value < 6.0). The two disagree on NaN: value >= 6.0 is false for NaN, ~(value < 6.0) is true. A NaN row was therefore returned only when another value in its file kept the file from being skipped:
# file 1: value [NaN, 7.0] (ids 1, 2); file 2: value [NaN, 5.0] (ids 3, 4)
tbl.scan(row_filter="not value < 6.0").to_arrow()  # ids [1, 2]: the NaN of file 2 is skipped with its file
tbl.scan(row_filter="value >= 6.0").to_arrow()     # ids [2]
This change applies rewrite_not to the bound file filter in _task_to_record_batches too, so rows are filtered with the same predicates that decided which files to read, and NOT no longer reaches Arrow. Only negated range comparisons on NaN change: the other negations (=, IN, IS NULL, IS NaN, STARTS WITH) give the same Arrow result before and after the rewrite.
Follow-up from the review of #4346, as suggested by @Fokko.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_scan_negated_comparison_matches_file_pruning_for_nan in tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py scans a file that is read and a file that is skipped, both holding a NaN row, with not value < 6.0, not (value < 6.0 and id = 1) and their rewritten forms, on each catalog of the catalog fixture. It fails without this change.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes: a scan whose filter negates a range comparison on a float or double column no longer returns NaN rows, which matches the file-level filtering. No API changes.
This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.

A server that serializes unset fields as null makes the table and view create/load/register responses fail with a pydantic validation error, because TableResponse.config, TableResponse.storage_credentials and ViewResponse.config only default when the key is absent. body:
Rationale for this change
In v1 table metadata the partition field ids were not tracked: the spec says they were "assigned sequentially in each spec starting at 1,000". A v1 partition-spec (or partition-specs entry) whose fields have no field-id currently fails to parse: a pydantic "Field required" error for one field, and TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'NoneType' for two or more, raised while computing last-partition-id.
TableMetadataV1.construct_partition_specs now assigns 1000, 1001, ... within each spec when none of its fields has an id, before computing last-partition-id. A spec that mixes fields with and without ids is rejected with Java's message ("Cannot parse spec with missing field IDs"), as in PartitionSpecParser.

Yes, test_v1_partition_fields_without_field_id in tests/table/test_metadata.py (fails on main, passes here). Also ran tests/table, tests/test_serializers.py, tests/catalog/test_base.py and tests/catalog/test_sql.py.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Old v1 tables written without partition field ids can now be loaded.

body:
Closes #4355
Rationale for this change
When a partition field is removed (update_spec().remove_field(...)) and its source column is later dropped (update_schema().delete_column(...)), historical partition specs and manifests still reference the dropped source_id.
Previously:

TableMetadata.specs_struct() only queried self.schema().find_type(field.source_id), causing ValueError in entries(), partitions(), files(), data_files(), delete_files(), all_files(), all_data_files(), and all_delete_files().
InspectTable._generate_manifests_table() evaluated spec.partition_type(self.tbl.schema()), which resolved dropped source columns as UnknownType() and rendered historical partition_summaries bounds as 'null'.

This change updates TableMetadata.specs_struct() to fall back through historical schemas in reversed(self.schemas) (and UnknownType() only if absent from all schemas), and updates InspectTable._generate_manifests_table() to reuse specs_struct([spec.spec_id]).

body:
Rationale for this change
add_files looks up each Parquet column path in a mapping built from the table's current column names, so a file that is valid for the table fails when its paths differ from those names:
catalog.create_table("db.t", schema=Schema(NestedField(1, "a", LongType()), NestedField(2, "b", StringType())))
with catalog.load_table("db.t").update_schema() as update:
    update.rename_column("a", "c")
# The file has field IDs 1 and 2, and column 1 is still named "a" in it.
catalog.load_table("db.t").add_files(["a.parquet"])  # KeyError: 'a'
The same happens for a nested field renamed after the file was written (KeyError: 'address.zip') and for a list whose element is named item, the layout pyarrow writes with use_compliant_nested_type=False (KeyError: 'tags.list.item'). #716 reported the list case; the stale bot closed it without a fix.
The name-based mapping can also record statistics under the wrong column. If the table drops a (field ID 1) and adds a new a (field ID 3), an old file's a is recorded under field ID 3, so a scan for a IS NULL prunes the file and misses its rows.
This change builds the mapping from the file's own column paths and field IDs (with name mapping for files without IDs), so statistics follow field IDs as they do for files PyIceberg writes.
Are these changes tested?
Yes, in tests/io/test_pyarrow.py. test_add_files_matches_columns_by_field_id covers the nested rename and the item list element with and without field IDs. test_add_files_rejects_columns_missing_from_table covers a file column whose field ID the table lacks and a column whose name matches but whose field ID differs. Both fail without this change.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes:

add_files accepts files whose columns were renamed in the table and files whose list element is not named element.
A file column whose field ID is not in the table now gets the existing "PyArrow table contains more columns" ValueError instead of a KeyError.
A file column whose name matches a table column but whose field ID differs is rejected with the same error. Before, such a file was added with its statistics under the wrong column.

Rationale for this change
Table.append fails for a table identity-partitioned on a uuid column:

body:
Rationale for this change
Table.snapshot_as_of_timestamp walks the snapshot log backwards and returns the first entry at or before the timestamp, which assumes the log is ordered by timestamp. The spec does not guarantee that, and Java's TableMetadata accepts a log entry up to one minute older than the previous one, so inside that skew window the lookup can return an older snapshot. Java fixed the same assumption in SnapshotUtil.nullableSnapshotIdAsOfTime (apache/iceberg#17360, "finding the entry with the maximum timestamp <= requested timestamp").
This picks the entry with the largest timestamp that is at or before (or strictly before, with inclusive=False) the requested one. On equal timestamps the later entry wins, unlike Java which keeps the first: PyIceberg logs every snapshot added in one transaction with its own timestamp_ms, so two can share a millisecond and the later one is the state that was actually current. Later-wins is also what PyIceberg and Java did before. inspect.metadata_log_entries uses the same lookup for latest_snapshot_id.
Are these changes tested?
Yes, test_snapshot_by_timestamp_with_unordered_snapshot_log in tests/table/test_init.py (two entries 10 seconds out of order, plus a tie; fails on main, passes here). tests/table/test_init.py and tests/table/test_inspect.py pass.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Time travel by timestamp returns the right snapshot when the snapshot log has entries slightly out of timestamp order.
title: Pick the latest timestamp in snapshot_as_of_timestamp instead of the last log entry

When a snapshot is removed (RemoveSnapshotsUpdate, which expire_snapshots uses), pyiceberg removes the snapshot's statistics files but keeps its partition statistics files. After expiring a snapshot, the table metadata still has partition-statistics entries pointing at a snapshot that is gone.

body:
Rationale for this change
Scan planning gets uuid identity partitions wrong. On a table partitioned by identity(u) on a uuid column:
tbl.scan(row_filter=EqualTo("u", str(first))).plan_files()   # no files; count() is 0
tbl.scan(row_filter=In("u", {str(first), str(second)})).plan_files()  # no files
tbl.scan(row_filter=NotEqualTo("u", str(first))).count()     # counts the excluded partition too
Manifests are read with uuid partition values as uuid.UUID, while a UUIDLiteral holds the 16 bytes, so the partition evaluator and the residual evaluator compare a UUID with bytes and never find them equal. EqualTo and In plan no files, and NotEqualTo and NotIn plan every file. Engines that use PyIceberg's planning (plan_files()) get the same wrong set of files, and count() is wrong because it trusts the residual.
This change gives partition values the representation literals use (a uuid becomes its 16 bytes) before the partition and residual evaluators compare them. It only applies to specs with a uuid partition field; other partition values are passed through unchanged.
Follow-up to #4360, which noted this as a separate fix. Reading the matching files still hits the PyArrow ArrowNotImplementedError of #2372: to_arrow() raises it, and so does count() when it has to read the files (a row predicate that the partition does not resolve, or delete files). For = and in filters this replaces silently returning no rows.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_scan_plans_uuid_identity_partitions in tests/io/test_pyarrow.py, next to the append test from #4360, checks the planned partitions and count() for =, in, != and not in filters on a uuid identity partition. It fails on main (the = filter plans no files) and passes with this change.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Bug fix: the partition and residual evaluators compare uuid partition values with uuid literals correctly. No API changes.
This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.
title: Fix filters on a table identity-partitioned on a uuid column

body:
Rationale for this change
The row filter parser rejects two kinds of valid numeric literals:
tbl.scan(row_filter="price > 1e-3")
# ParseException: Expected end of text, found 'e'  (at char 9), (line:1, col:10)
tbl.scan(row_filter="quantity in (1, 2.5)")
# ParseException: Expected ')', found '.'  (at char 17), (line:1, col:18)
Decimal literals used pyparsing's common.real(), which has no exponent, so 1e-3 parses as 1 and the rest is left over. A literal set had to be all decimals or all integers, so a list that mixes 1 and 2.5 did not parse either.
This change uses common.sci_real(), which accepts everything common.real() does plus an exponent (1e-3, -1.5E3, 2.5e1), and lets a literal set mix integers and decimals. Integers become LongLiterals and decimal or exponent forms become DecimalLiterals; binding uses the existing conversion rules (a decimal column needs a literal with its scale, and an integer column rejects fractional values). The decimal parse action already builds the Decimal from the matched text, so exponents are exact. A list that mixes numbers with strings still raises a ParseException (test_in_different_types).
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_scientific_notation and test_in_mixed_numbers in tests/expressions/test_parser.py cover exponents on either side of a comparison and in BETWEEN, and mixed integer/decimal IN lists (in both orders) and NOT IN lists. Both fail on main with the ParseExceptions above and pass with this change.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Bug fix: row filter strings accept scientific notation and IN lists that mix integers and decimals. Expressions that parsed before parse to the same result.
This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.

Rationale for this change
A float filter on a wide decimal column raises decimal.InvalidOperation:
# amt is decimal(38, 2)
tbl.scan(row_filter=GreaterThan("amt", 1e26)).to_arrow()
# decimal.InvalidOperation: [<class 'decimal.InvalidOperation'>]

# amt is decimal(38, 30)
tbl.scan(row_filter=LessThan("amt", 0.5)).to_arrow()
# decimal.InvalidOperation: [<class 'decimal.InvalidOperation'>]
FloatLiteral.to(DecimalType) and DoubleLiteral.to(DecimalType) quantize the value to the column's scale under the default decimal context, which keeps 28 digits. When the quantized value has more digits than that (1e26 with 2 decimals, or 0.5 with 30 decimals), quantize raises. A decimal column can hold up to 38 digits, so these are valid filters.
This change quantizes under a local context with enough precision for the result, in one helper used by both conversions. Rounding is unchanged (ROUND_HALF_UP), and positive and negative infinity still raise the ValueError added in #4287 for #4286. NaN remains rejected when a literal is constructed.

Closes #4291.
Rationale for this change
Follow-up to #4292, which handled the rewrite itself. This covers the retry conflict check from the issue.
When a commit retries, _validate_no_new_deletes_for_data_files checks that no new delete file applies to the data files being replaced. It built its delete index with the operation's filter, though, so _filter_manifest_entries skipped any delete file whose column bounds can't match that filter. A partial delete rewrites those data files in full, so a concurrent delete outside the filter went unnoticed. The retry then committed the rewritten file, and the rows that delete removed came back.
Now every delete file added since the starting snapshot is checked against the replaced data files. The filter is no longer used there, so data_filter and case_sensitive are dropped from the private function's signature. _validate_no_new_delete_files, the filter-based check, is unchanged.
Are these changes tested?

a stale table handle starts delete("k = 1");
meanwhile, a position delete storing the row (2, 'b') is committed. It has bounds k = 2, built with commit_partition_position_delete;
the retried delete must raise ValidationException, leaving k = [1, 3].

Without the fix, the test fails with DID NOT RAISE ValidationException, because the retry commits over the concurrent delete.
Are there any user-facing changes?

body:
Rationale for this change
When a REST server omits residual-filter from a file scan task, PyIceberg treats the task as unfiltered. For a Parquet file with x = [1, 2, 1], scan(row_filter="x != 1").count() returns 3 while to_arrow() returns 1.
Use the original scan filter as the fallback residual for both the initial plan and any fetched task batches, as required by the Iceberg REST specification. Explicit server residuals still take precedence.
This addresses the REST case reported in #4278.
Are these changes tested?
The regression uses a local Parquet file and exercises both the initial response and pagination. It fails on main and the current head of #4278, and passes with this change. The planning tests also verify that an explicit true residual is preserved and that an unfiltered request still gets an unfiltered task.
make test: 4,685 passed, 5 skipped. make lint passed.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Filtered counts now agree with Arrow scans when a server omits the residual. Affected files may be read to apply the filter.
AI assistance
An AI assistant helped trace the planning code and draft the tests; I reviewed and ran everything and take responsibility for the change.
